*Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*, Original Text, Chapter Thirty-five:
The Bodhisattva Grounds—Seeking Great Enlightenment. Out of compassion for sentient beings, one seeks bodhi, aspiring with a resolute vow.
Firm and courageous,
having cultivated and realized [the path] over a long period of time,
they have forever transcended the world.
Because they possess great conduct and great fruits, they are called Bodhisattvas. Thus,
the lineage of a Bodhisattva, the generation of the mind of awakening, the practice, and the attainment of the fruit—
all these taken together are collectively termed the "Bodhisattva-bhūmi."
Within this, there are four bases of yoga (*yogasthāna*).
The *Dizhi jing* (Bhūmivastu) refers to them as "bases of skillful means" (*upāyasthāna*),
while the present text calls them "yoga."
The correct translation is "correspondence" (*yoga*).
Its meaning is as previously explained.
Regarding the phrase "four yogas":
First is the Yoga of Retention (*dhāraṇā-yoga*).
This sets forth the dharmas realized by those bodhisattvas;
whether cause or fruit, they are collectively termed the first station of the yoga of retention.
Second is the yoga of following the dharma (*anulomika-yoga*);
that is, it is called "following the dharma" because it arises as a practice in accordance with the aforementioned dharma.
Third is the yoga of ultimate attainment (*niṣṭhā-yoga*).
Because it is perfected through cultivation, it is called "ultimate.
This is the fourth sequential yoga of retention.
First, the section on yoga further clarifies the preceding meaning.
This means that they are called "sequential" because of the sequence of their categories.
The term "sustaining" (dhāraṇa) refers to upholding;
this has three meanings.
First, the cause sustains the fruit;
second, the shadowy clouds sustain their own substance.
Baoliang said:
"To be capable is called 'upholding' (dhāraṇa).
Those who possess the spiritual lineage (gotra) are so called because they possess this capability."
Third, the former is able to sustain the latter,
as in the initial yoga; subsequently,
there are three types of sustenance.
First is the maintenance of the spiritual lineage;
this involves maintaining the arousal of the bodhicitta and maintaining the skillful means of practice.
Through maintaining the arousal of the bodhicitta and maintaining the skillful means of practice, the fruit of Buddhahood is produced.
Ce says: "Holding" has three meanings;
namely, holding the fruit by means of the cause.
It is distinguished by its function as a total retention (dhāraṇī). Because it retains the meaning through the words,
it is called "retention" (dhāraṇī).
The general discussion comprises eighteen chapters in total.
The "Chapter on Spiritual Lineage" (*gotra-varga*) is at the beginning; thus it is called the first.
According to the Sanskrit manuscript:
In the original [Sanskrit] text, the first word was at the bottom;
however, following the convention of this region, the first word is placed at the top, hence it says "First Yoga" and so forth, up to "The First. Question:
Regarding the three preceding types of vidyādhara practices and all their myriad activities:
what is the distinction between the three stages of illumination?
Is it that they are illuminated through three cycles?
The record states:
As the son of the most excellent [Maitreya], the master of the Yoga school,
explained the first twelve stages of the Vidyādhara.
These are solely the dharmas of practice to be undertaken.
Second, the thirteen stages (*trayodaśa-vihāra*) of illumination according to the Dharma,
which also include the explanation of the Tathāgata-stage (*tathāgata-vihāra*).
This clarifies the method for practicing [the stages].
Second, the ultimate synthesis combines the thirteen abodes (*vihāra*) into seven grounds (*bhūmi*).
What are these seven grounds?
From the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) up to the ultimate goal,
this period clarifies that learning has been perfected;
it further elucidates cause and effect.
Although the meaning is elucidated through three cycles,
their purports differ;
for the sake of this section on the stages (*bhūmi*), they are collectively judged as two.
First, the preceding section establishes what follows, while the latter two provide the formal explanation.
Tai states: "This is based on the version of the sūtra from the Western Regions."
First, regarding the scribe who transcribes the scriptures:
when about to transcribe the scriptures,
they may first take refuge in the Triple Gem.
Alternatively, some may have previously taken refuge in Maheśvara;
however, in the old translations of this section,
the verse on taking refuge by the Master of the Treatise (Śāstrakāra) was erroneously placed here.
Furthermore, it is a profound error to claim that the *Uddāna* was produced after the outflows and fetters (*āsrava-saṃyojana*) had already arisen.
If the Master first paid homage to the Buddhas of the three times before composing this treatise, [then...]
The words of taking refuge should appear at the beginning of the treatise, prior to the section on the five groups of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, according to the Sanskrit manuscript,
the beginning of each chapter contains a summary of what preceded and an introduction to what follows, as well as a general verse.
Why does the *Dharmaskandha* not follow the previous examples and omit this? It is clear,
therefore, that it is the Master of the Sūtra (*Sūtrakāra*) who pays homage to the Buddhas of the three times,
and not the Master of the Treatise (*Śāstrakāra*).
Within the formal explanation,
one first elucidates the first three yogas consisting of twenty-seven chapters; that is,
the explanation of the three supports (*ādhāra*) and ten dharmas.
The third section explains the fourth yoga,
which consists of the sequential order of the twenty-seven chapters of the introduction.
This fourth [section] is not found in the text of the old treatise.
Within the preceding section, there are again three parts:
first, ten dharmas are presented to briefly indicate the essential framework;
second, based on questions, they are analyzed in detail.
The third section concludes the explanation.
Within the preceding [section], first, a single verse is cited to list the names of the ten dharmas;
second, the prose commentary assigns them accordingly.
Regarding the statement that "ten factors fully encompass the Mahāyāna bodhisattva path and its fruits," according to the terminology of the Sanskrit original,
this is far removed from [the teachings of] Dharmatrāta.

In the language of Tang [Chinese], there are ten terms: *sattva* (being), *phalasattva* (fruit-being), *sattva* (sentient being), *mārga* (path), *bodhi* (awakening), *mahāyāna* (Great Vehicle), *saṃgha* (community), *arhant* (worthy one), *śikṣā* (training), and *kṣānti* (patience). Now, following these terms: 1. **Sattva**: This refers to the three types of beings (*trividha-sattva*). First, the "ordinary being" (*pṛthagjana-sattva*), who has not yet attained the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and has not yet produced the supramundane mind; they are called "beings" because they are bound by the fetters of birth and death. Second, the "fruit-being" (*phala-sattva*), who has already entered the path of seeing and has attained the fruit of the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) up to arhatship; they are called "beings" because they have already attained the fruits of the path. Third, the "sentient being" (*sattva-sattva*), who has already entered the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and has attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) up to the stage of the Buddha; they are called "beings" because they possess the nature of a sentient being, which is the seed of the Tathāgata’s wisdom. 2. **Mārga**: This refers to the four paths. First, the "path of accumulation" (*sambhāramārga*), which comprises the five roots of faith and so forth, the five powers, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Second, the "path of preparation" (*prayogamārga*), which is the stage of heat (*uṣmagata*) and the others within the four stages of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). Third, the "path of seeing" (*darśanamārga*), which is the stage of the sixteen moments of mind that realize the four noble truths. Fourth, the "path of cultivation" (*bhāvanāmārga*), which is the stage from the second dhyāna of the path of seeing up to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*). 3. **Bodhi**: This refers to the three types of awakening. First, the "awakening of the śrāvaka," which is the realization of the four noble truths through the sixteen aspects. Second, the "awakening of the pratyekabuddha," which is the realization of the twelve links of dependent origination through the twenty-four aspects. Third, the "unsurpassed complete perfect awakening" (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), which is the realization of all phenomena through the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. 4. **Mahāyāna**: This refers to the Great Vehicle. It is called "great" because it possesses five greatnesses: the greatness of its object (*ālambana*), the greatness of its aspiration (*adhimukti*), the greatness of its practice (*pratipatti*), the greatness of its skillful means (*upāya*), and the greatness of its ultimate attainment (*samudāgama*). 5. **Saṃgha**: This refers to the community. It is called "community" because it consists of those who have gathered together in harmony, sharing the same precepts, the same views, the same conduct, and the same livelihood. 6. **Arhant**: This refers to the worthy one. They are called "worthy" because they have eliminated all faults and are worthy of receiving offerings from gods and humans. 7. **Śikṣā**: This refers to training. There are three trainings: the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*), the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*), and the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*). 8. **Kṣānti**: This refers to patience. There are three patiences: patience regarding the Dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharma-kṣānti*), patience regarding subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), and patience regarding the Dharma of cessation (*nirodhadharma-kṣānti*). 9. **Dāna**: This refers to giving. There are three kinds of giving: the giving of wealth, the giving of fearlessness, and the giving of the Dharma. 10. **Yajña**: This refers to sacrifice. It is the act of making offerings to the Three Jewels with a pure heart. Thus, these ten terms are explained according to their respective meanings.
This demonstrates that these ten dharmas fully encompass the entirety of the causal and resultant teachings of the Mahāyāna;
thus, it is said they "completely include the Mahāyāna.
What, then, is this Mahāyāna?
This refers to the path and its fruit.
Because the *pūrvasābdika* (one who has already completed the training) is [already] established, the fruit is not mentioned separately.
Within the explanation, there is further inclusion.
Moreover, according to the Sanskrit original, there are seven case endings (*vibhakti*).
There are ten factors that fully encompass the first case ending (*prathamā-vibhakti*).
This refers to being able to encompass the Mahāyāna bodhisattva path and its fruition;
it is that which is encompassed because of the sixth case (the genitive).
However, the earlier translators did not understand this shift in grammatical case.
"Therefore, the Mahāyāna is the grasper,
and the ten dharmas are the grasped.
This, too, is erroneous.
Next, ten dharmas are enumerated.
First is "retention" (*dhāraṇī*),
which consists of three types of retention.
The two characteristics are the five characteristics of a bodhisattva;
the three divisions.
In Sanskrit it is called *varga*;
in this language [Chinese] it is called "chapter" (*pin*),
or alternatively "section" (*fen*) or "wing" (*yi*).
Among the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-dharmāḥ*), this same term also occurs;
thus it is likewise translated as "part" (*aṅga*).
It is also translated as "chapter" (*varga*).
The old translation "Wing" (Yì) is erroneous.
This section does not explain the meaning of having many wings;
rather, it clarifies the difference between the two categories of Bodhisattvas: those who remain at home and those who have left the household life.
Therefore, it is called by its old title.
If that were so, then at the time of titling a chapter, it would simultaneously be titled "Chapter on Chapters," which presents this mutual contradiction.
Therefore, it is called "classification.

Fourth, the Sanskrit term for "ground" is *bhūmi*; "superior" (*adhimātra*) and "intention" (*āśaya*) are collectively termed "superior intention" (*adhyāśaya*), which refers to the fifteen types of intention. The Sanskrit term for "mind" is *citta*, which is translated here as "pure mind."
This expression is also not found in the ten dharmas of the Sanskrit original.
The five abodes are,
in fact, the thirteen abodes.
Sixth is birth,
which refers to the five modes of birth by which bodhisattvas transform sentient beings.
Seventh is gathering [disciples].
In Sanskrit, what is meant by "Brahma"? Among the ten dharmas of the Brahmakāyika devas, this name also does not appear.
The eighth stage is, in fact, the sixth stage.
Nine practices,
which are the four types of practice of a bodhisattva;
ten establishments.
In Sanskrit it is called *pratītyasamutpāda*.
It is so named because it establishes the one hundred and forty virtues of the Tathāgata.
It is also called *vipaśyanā*.
This is translated as "establishment" (an-lì),
though it does not exist in this way in the Sanskrit original.
The ten dharmas are analyzed according to their meaning into six categories.
First is the general and the specific.
The former tradition states that the first precept is the general,
while the remaining nine are the specific.
Now, the Tripitaka Master says:
This treatise takes ten dharmas as its essence.
Among these ten dharmas, those that encompass all phenomena are termed "comprehensive" (saṃgraha).
That which is not fully subsumed is called "particular" (viśeṣa).
Because "abiding" (sthiti) and "stages" (bhūmi) universally subsume both cause and effect, they are called "general" (sāmānya).
The remaining eight types do not universally subsume cause and effect, and are therefore called "particular."
Second is the analysis of cause and effect.
Regarding this, there are various explanations by former masters in their treatises on doctrine; here is my own interpretation.
The first type is solely a cause and not a fruit;
the eleventh type is solely a fruit and not a cause.
This applies to both their abiding and their stages.
This encompasses both cause and effect;
as for the remaining six types,
according to the textual presentation, they are described as being only causes and not effects.
In terms of ultimate reality, all are applicable to both cause and effect.
Third, regarding the distinction between the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi-vibhāga*):
these four are established as stages based on the sustaining ground (*dhṛti-bhūmi*).
The remaining six are formations (*saṃskāra*).
Speaking generally, they all pertain to the stage of practice (*pratipad*).
Fourth is benefiting oneself and others.
It was previously stated that the first five are for one's own benefit,
while the subsequent three are for the benefit of others.
The latter two pertain to the benefit of oneself and others. Generally speaking,
the cultivation of all ten dharmas is termed self-benefit.
The ten kinds of benefiting others are all termed "benefiting others" (parārtha).
Now, according to the characteristics of the lower section of the treatise,
the first five are for one's own benefit (svārtha).
The first three benefit both oneself and others;
the latter two benefit others alone.
Fifth is the excellence of self-perfection.
The ancient commentary states:
"The first eight are self-perfection;
the latter two are superior progress."
If one were to claim that all ten factors, when accomplished, are exclusively "one's own portion" (svabhāga),
and that practicing them upward is exclusively "superior progress" (viśeṣagamana),
this interpretation is incorrect.
The treatise states that there is no distinct characteristic [between them].
Of these, the first lineage is exclusively its own specific category (*svaviśeṣa*),
while the remaining nine are both its own specific category and its superior progress (*viśeṣābhyudgama*).
That which precedes the expectation is "superior progress" (viśeṣa), and that which follows the expectation is "one's own portion" (svabhāga).
Sixth is the distinction of the three types of maintenance (trividha-dhāraṇa).
There are two kinds of these three types of maintenance.
Regarding the three types of retention— initial, ultimate, and intermediate—
the New Treatise (Xinlun) actually possesses four types of retention;
for now, we shall set aside the fourth, sequential retention.
To speak according to ultimate reality,
these three types of sustenance collectively encompass ten dharmas.
However, among these ten, the power of cultivation in the first eighteen categories is inferior.
The initial arising of syllables is called the "first retention" (*ādhāra*).
Following this, there are the four categories beginning with "conformity to the Dharma" (*anuloma-yoga*) and "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*).
When the power of cultivation and practice is strong and their application gradually becomes superior,
it is called "intermediate retention."
The ultimate yoga having been transcended,
the five categories beginning with birth gradually reach fulfillment through cultivation.
When one attains the fruit and draws near to it,
it is called "ultimate upholding.
Master Yuǎn also provides this interpretation.
The two types of lineage, the arousal of the thought of enlightenment, and the application are distinguished by three supports.
The first support is the Dharma;
in meaning, it corresponds to the lineage (*gotra*).
The four meanings beginning with "subsequent characteristics" correspond to the stage of generating the resolve;
the five meanings beginning with "subsequent arising" correspond to what follows.
These should be maintained through preparatory application.
If discussed in general terms, however,
all ten dharmas are common to all three types of maintenance.
Just as the sense of abiding and maintaining within a lineage is called "sustenance" (dhṛti),
the sense of manifesting and representing is called "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa).
The meaning of "tending toward" is precisely this "wings of the Dharma.
Partial realization and freedom from defilement are termed the "pure mind."
The establishment of a state through the perfection of virtue is also what constitutes "abiding.
Relying on the retribution [of the body] and conforming to external objects, it is designated as "birth."
Gathering and transforming sentient beings is itself the gathering of the Dharma.
When the stage of benefiting others is perfected, it is called a "ground" (bhūmi).
When superior cultivation progresses upward, it is termed "practice" (caryā).
To realize the reality according to the words is called "establishment.
Since this is the case for the spiritual lineage (*gotra*),
the same explanation applies by analogy to the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) and the skillful means (*upāya*).
The preceding section has already explained the general outline and essential framework.
From here on, the second part provides a detailed analysis according to specific categories.
This text is divided into three distinct sections.
First, the explanation of the meaning of the first *dhāraṇī* (retention).
Within this, it is extensively expanded into eighteen chapters;
this constitutes the first yoga.
Next, the explanation of the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) regarding the aspects (*lakṣaṇa*) and the abiding in the four dharmas constitutes four chapters;
this is the second [section], the yoga that accords with the dharma (*anudharmayoga*).
Next, the explanation of the establishment of the stages of practice (*caryā-pratisthāpana*) within the ground of birth and inclusion (*janma-saṃgraha-bhūmi*) constitutes five chapters.
This is the third, the ultimate yoga.
These three yogas are respectively the initial holding, the subsequent holding, and the ultimate holding.
There is no separate teaching for the fourth yoga.
Question: Why is the first among these "upholdings" (dhāraṇīs) given that name? Answer:
Because within this category of upholdings, three types of upholding are clarified:
first, the spiritual lineage (gotra).
Second is capability;
third are the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
These three meanings are termed "retaining" (*dhāraṇa*).
The extensive explanation is as such;
therefore, one attains the "holding of the name.
Now, these three types of holding will be briefly analyzed by way of three gates.
First, the discernment of essence:
the initial lineage takes the two types of lineage as its essence;
the arousal of the mind takes the great vow as its essence.
Aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) is seeking.
Thus, superior understanding (*adhimukti*), desire (*chanda*), faith (*śraddhā*), and reflection (*cintā*) all involve seeking.
However, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that "the latter four perfections are the wisdom of the latter [stage]."
Since this wisdom is defined as that which guides and provides a general judgment,
how could it lack a distinct substantial entity?
It is like the teaching that the first six perfections are subsumed within non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
How could there not be distinct entities for giving, morality, and so forth?
The Bodhipakṣa-dharmas (factors conducive to enlightenment) take the six perfections and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as their essence.
Second, the clarification of names.
There are both general and specific [meanings].
Regarding the general name "the three supports" (tri-dhāraṇī):
"three" is a numerical term, and "support" (dhāraṇī) is a term for its meaning.
The three meanings of "possessing" have been explained above.
As for the specific names:
The two lineages constitute the lineage;
up to and including the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), which constitute the third support.
Therefore, all are designated by names according to their respective essential natures.
Alternatively, all may be designated according to their functional significance.
Regarding the distinctions between the stages and levels of the three types of knowledge (*vidyā*), Cè states that there are two meanings.
First, to discuss them according to their actual reality:
Prior to the ten stages of faith, there is only the lineage (gotra).
From the ten stages of faith onward, up to the diamond-like samādhi (vajropama-samādhi), all possess the three types of sustenance.
Second, the discussion of the three [stages] based on their assigned positions.
In the Western lands, there are three differing explanations.
One interpretation holds that the stage prior to the ten levels of faith is called the "retention of the lineage" (gotra-dhāraṇa),
while the ten levels of faith constitute the "retention of the arousal of the mind" (cittotpāda-dhāraṇa).
From the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*) onward, they are maintained as the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
The second [text] states that from time immemorial up until the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), they are maintained as the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
The reason for this is as follows:
The two types—the innate nature (*prakṛti*) and acquired habituation (*abhyāsa*)—constitute the support for the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
From the ten stages of understanding (*adhimukti*) up to the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), they constitute the support for the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*).
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama*), they constitute the support for the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
The third section, the "Cloud Division," divides the three *kalpas* into three stages of sustenance (*dhāraṇī*).
Specifically, from the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) upward through the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* constitutes the first stage of sustenance.
From the first *bhūmi* upward through the seventh *bhūmi* constitutes the second stage of sustenance.
From the eighth stage upward, the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa constitutes the third upholding.
Jì (基) states that there are two traditions in the West.
One interpretation states:

the "upholding of the lineage" (*gotra-dhāraṇa*) refers to that which Bodhisattva Ratnacandra took as the beginningless, naturally abiding lineage (*anādikālikadharmatā-gotra*), namely, prior to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*);
the "upholding of the resolve" (*cittotpāda-dhāraṇa*) refers to all instances of generating the resolve from the ten stages of faith onward.
The "sustaining of the factors of enlightenment" refers to the practices undertaken from the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) onward;
the meaning and scope of this are the same as those for the Bodhisattva who protects the Dharma.
There is a slight difference, however, in the interpretation of the master Vasumitra.
What is meant by "distinctly"?

It refers to the lineage (*gotra*) which is maintained; that is, the quality of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that have existed since beginningless time and are capable of being severed is designated as "lineage.
This means that within the locus where those obstructions can be severed, there exist untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*).
When one generates the mind and undertakes the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), the *śruta-mayī-prajñā*, *cintā-mayī-prajñā*, and so forth, which are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*),
as well as the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), are identical in meaning to those previously described.
Furthermore, there is another distinct explanation.
First, the maintenance of the lineage (*gotra*), which refers to the stage prior to the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Second, the maintenance of the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), which refers to the stages from the ten levels of faith onward.
Third, the maintenance of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), which refers to the stages from the ten levels of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*) onward.
Furthermore, it is said:
the "support of the lineage" refers to the ten stages of faith;
the "support of the arousal of the bodhicitta" refers to the stage of ten understandings.
Although there is this explanation that the "sustenance" (dhāraṇa) of the factors conducive to enlightenment refers to the stage of the ten practices,
no one has yet lingered over it.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that it is not based [on the lineage]. How, then, can it be relied upon?
Furthermore, "upholding the lineage" refers to the naturally abiding lineage (*dharmatā-gotra*).

The generation of the mind [of awakening] can be attained both at the initial generation of the mind ten *kalpas* prior to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) and by the true generation of the bodhicitta upon reaching the first stage (*bhūmi*). Within this context,
if one were to provide a general structural analysis, it would constitute the first yoga.
Furthermore, the first seventeen chapters correctly explain the characteristics of the Bodhisattva-bhūmi,
while the final chapter sets forth the merit of receiving and upholding [this teaching] to encourage others to practice and study it;
otherwise, it would not be so.
It is directly judged that within the first yoga there are three dhāraṇīs.
Regarding the explanation of these three dhāraṇīs,
the text consists of two parts.
First, the three types of *dhṛti* (sustenance) are briefly distinguished;
second, from "What is lineage (*gotra*)" onwards, they are extensively distinguished.
Within the former [section], as for the question "What is meant by *dhṛti*? and so forth:
This brief dialogue sets forth the essence of the three types of sustenance (*dhṛti*).
That is to say, for those bodhisattvas who possess the lineage of their own vehicle, this is the sustenance of the lineage (*gotra-dhṛti*).
To distinguish them from those of the two vehicles, they are called bodhisattvas.
Although bodhisattvas may also possess the seeds of the two vehicles,
because they take only the Mahāyāna seeds as their lineage-holding essence, it is called "one's own vehicle."
The first generation of the mind of awakening is itself the second generation of the mind of awakening as maintenance.
Although it is known that the generation of the mind of awakening extends from the beginning to the end,
it is referred to here as "the first" because this is stated according to what is most preeminent.
Regarding the mention of "all factors conducive to enlightenment" (bodhipakṣadharma), this refers to the third practice: maintaining through skillful means. Why is this so?
Because the meaning of "maintaining" will be explained below.

Regarding the statement, "Because Bodhisattvas take their own vehicle's lineage as their support and foundation, they possess capability and great power," Jing says: This clarifies that by taking the two types of lineage as a basis, one is able to attain bodhi.
Because it serves as a basis, it can be established;
because it is established, it possesses capability;
because it possesses capability, it has great power.
Because one is endowed with such qualities as these, one attains bodhi.
Furthermore, "being capable" explains the aforementioned reliance (*niśraya*),
and "possessing great power" explains the aforementioned establishment (*vyavasthāna*).
Master Ji says: "In explaining this passage now, I shall provisionally offer two interpretations.
First, because one relies upon the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), there is a capacity and power that enables the attainment of enlightenment;
that is, it is precisely because the spiritual lineage possesses this capacity and power that one can establish great enlightenment."
Second, because they rely upon their own vehicle’s lineage (*gotra*), they possess the capacity to achieve perfect enlightenment;
and because their own vehicle’s lineage serves as the foundation for their establishment, they possess great power to realize great bodhi.
The lineage (*gotra*) serves as the basis for these two explanations.
This is also stated in the subsequent explanation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) within the context of generating the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*).
As for the statement, "by means of which the bodhisattvas [possess] even up to that which is held as the great awakening to be perfected":
If the "auspicious clouds" (kṣetra-megha) are complete, they belong to the cause and are thus the capacity for fulfillment;
if they are fulfilled, they belong to the result and are thus that which is fulfilled.
Since it is said that they are "that which is fulfilled," one should know that they belong to the result.
Question: Among the three, beginning with the spiritual lineage (gotra),
one type serves as the support.
Why is it that the spiritual lineage (gotra) itself sustains the fruit of Buddhahood;
that the arousal of the mind of enlightenment (cittotpāda) sustains the skillful means of practice;
and that these skillful means of practice sustain the fruit of Buddhahood?
The commentary states:
This is an abbreviated presentation.
By adorning the meaning with various textual expressions, it becomes easy to understand.
Just as that spiritual lineage sustains the fruit of Buddhahood,
one should know that the generation of the resolve likewise sustains the fruit of Buddhahood;
since the generation of the resolve already sustains the subsequent practices and skillful means.
One should know that the lineage also sustains the subsequent arising of the mind of enlightenment;
the practice of skillful means sustains the fruit of Buddhahood.
Their meanings and functions are thus contiguous.
There is no need for laborious discrimination. Question:
This is a single type of abbreviated exposition.
Why is it not said that the arousal of the mind (cittotpāda) sustains the fruit of Buddhahood,
and that the spiritual lineage (gotra) sustains the arousal of the mind?
The explanation is as follows:
As for those who raise objections regarding meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is no need for further explanation; yet,
for those who must provide a thorough resolution, there is likewise a logical principle.
By virtue of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), that which is not yet fulfilled is the seed; this is the direct cause (*hetu*). Therefore, in relation to the fruit of Buddhahood, [it is the cause].
The initial arousal of the thought of enlightenment lasts for one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* and is characterized by outflows (*sāsrava*).
From the entry into the stages (*bhūmi*) onward, although it is without outflows (*anāsrava*),
because it is not the seed [of Buddhahood], it does not aspire toward the fruit of Buddhahood.
In the *Jinwang jiexing lun* (Treatise on the Stages of Practice for Approaching [Buddhahood]), there is a principle of "arising through mutual conditioning" used to distinguish their maintenance.
Tai states: "The initial nature-seed (*prakṛti-gotra*) serves as the basis for the bodhicitta, while the acquired seed-lineage (*samudānīta-gotra*) establishes the bodhicitta."
Because the nature-lineage (*prakṛti-gotra*) serves as its basis, it possesses capability;
because the cultivated lineage (*samudānīta-gotra*) serves as its establishment, it possesses great power.
Thus, the lineage-sustenance sustains the bodhicitta and leads to the distant realization of enlightenment.
Because the bodhicitta can attain awakening, it possesses the capacity for receptivity.
Second, the various spiritual lineages (gotra) can serve as the capacity for receptivity toward awakening;
therefore, they are designated by the name "capacity for receptivity" based on their result.
The second arousal of the mind arises from two lineages:
with respect to the sense of arising from the nature-lineage (*prakṛti-gotra*), it serves as the basis for the application of practice;
with respect to the sense of arising from the cultivated lineage (*paripuṣṭa-gotra*), it serves as the establishing cause for the application of practice.
However, practices such as giving and morality are termed "giving" and so forth when they occur prior to the ten stages of faith;
they are termed "pāramitās" when they occur within the ten stages of faith;
and they are termed "the two provisions" from the first bhūmi upward.
From the fourth bhūmi onwards, they are called "factors of enlightenment" (bodhipakṣa).
For this reason, the author of the treatise reiterates [the term].
Alternatively, one may speak of distinct names based on their simultaneous occurrence.
Because it closely counteracts the six hindrances,
because it enables one to ascend to the other shore,
and because it can support merit and wisdom.
Because it brings forth bodhi,
the third application arises from the nature-seed (prakṛti-gotra);
in meaning, it serves as the basis for great bodhi.
Because the stage of the lineage of practice (*śikṣāgotra*) serves as the establishing cause for great enlightenment,
it is able to bring the unsurpassed great awakening to full completion;
furthermore, because the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), which serve as its basis, are capable of sustaining enlightenment.
It is designated by way of its fruit:
it sustains the perfect great enlightenment,
even for those individuals who lack the spiritual lineage (agotra) or who are certainly incapable of fulfilling unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This cites the inferior to illustrate the superior. Jing asked:
"If there is no spiritual lineage (gotra), how can one generate the resolve for enlightenment, engage in the preparatory practices, and so forth?"
First interpretation:
This is a hypothetical statement.
Even if a person lacking the spiritual lineage (agotra) were to encounter a virtuous friend and resolve to practice, they would still be unable to realize unsurpassed bodhi.
How much more so for those who are unable to resolve their minds upon and practice such [virtues].
The second interpretation states:
even if a person lacking the spiritual lineage (agotra) were to resolve their mind and practice based on the seeds of merit (puṇyabhāga), [they would still fail].
Because these are with outflows (sāsrava),
one will ultimately be unable to attain unsurpassed bodhi.
A third interpretation states:
This refers to those of the two vehicles who lack the lineage of the Mahāyāna;
although they give rise to the mind of the two vehicles from their untainted seeds of the two vehicles and diligently cultivate the preparatory practices of the two vehicles,
they ultimately cannot attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
Tài says this is based on the explanation concerning those without the spiritual lineage (*agotra*) and those of the two vehicles with fixed natures (*niyata-gotra*).
Jī says there are three interpretations,
which he sets forth as a provisional discussion.
This is the first explanation.
It is determined that those of the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* lineages are also called "those without the Mahāyāna lineage.
Even though they may, according to conditions, give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), they are nonetheless incapable of accomplishing it.
Thus, it is said that although they have generated the resolve and so forth—
this is the second explanation—
that those individuals who by their very nature lack the potential (agotra), even if they truly generate the resolve, will ultimately regress and be unable to attain that unsurpassed enlightenment.
This is the third explanation.
Question: Since the arousal of the bodhicitta does not seek worldly fruits, from what kind of seed does this manifesting mind arise?
The commentary states:
It arises from the seeds of wholesome dharmas belonging to the category of merit;
it is not that the seeds of the untainted are non-existent.
Because they lack skillful means and untainted wisdom (anāsrava-prajñā),
the treatise states:
"They accomplish it solely through the roots of goodness of humans and devas," and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding what has already been called the "lineage" (gotra) as the "support" (dhṛti) and so forth:
it is also called the support for the arousal of the mind of awakening (cittotpāda), the support for the preparatory application (prayoga),
and even the dwelling-place (gṛha) of the lineage.
Regarding "the resolve as the dwelling" and "the application as the dwelling," Xuanzang states that according to the *Śāstra*, there are two interpretations.
One interpretation [applies these] to the six names beginning with "assistance."
These are all held as distinct names;
there is no further meaning beyond this.
There is also a distinction in the interpretation of their meanings.
It is called "retaining" (*dhāraṇa*) because it can sustain the fruit;
it is called "aiding" (*anugraha*) because it causes the fruit to continue to abide;
and it is called a "cause" (*hetu*) because it can produce the fruit.
It is called a "basis" (*niśraya*) because it serves as the support for the fruit;
it is called a "step" (*pratipadā*) because the fruit follows and is sustained by it;
and it is called a "precursor" (*pūrvamgama*) because it precedes the fruit.
It is called a "dwelling" (śālā) because it is the place where the fruit resides.
Zhiyi says: "Because it assists in the realization of the fruit."
Because it can produce a fruit;
because it relies on the attainment of a fruit;
and because it conforms to the [respective] stages.
Because it guides the arising of wisdom and because it contains the fruit,
these are respectively assigned to the auxiliary causes and so forth.
Question: What is the distinction between "practice" (*caryā*) and "application" (*prayoga*)? Answer:
Illuminating the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicittotpāda*) and maintaining it is called "application."
Now, this is also called "the application of the sphere of activity.
The commentary states:
the sphere of activity and the practitioner are two distinct types.
The practice that is undertaken refers to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*);
the practice that enables its undertaking refers to that generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*).
Therefore, the preceding generation of the mind is termed the "application of practice" (*prayoga*).
Now, according to the text, these are the two distinct types of practice: the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and the preparatory applications (*prayoga*).
Thus concludes the brief exposition of the three supports.
From here on, it will be explained in detail.
Thus, at the very beginning of the Chapter on Lineage (*gotra-varga*),
there is one chapter concerning lineage.
This explains the *Gotra-dhāraṇī*.
Second is the chapter on the "Arousing of the Resolve" (*Cittotpāda*), which explains the *Cittotpāda-dhāraṇī*.
After the final three chapters, there are sixteen chapters that collectively constitute the practice of skillful means and the upholding [of the teaching].
Within the Chapter on Lineage (Gotra), there are two parts.
The first section correctly defines the characteristics of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).

The second section provides a detailed analysis according to the meaning, from the bodhisattva of the spiritual lineage up to those who have not yet overcome the four secondary afflictions that are contrary to their own dharma.
According to the ancient school, this passage first concerns the stage of one's own nature (*svabhūmi*) and subsequently the stage of further progress (*viśeṣagamana*).
Within the former, there are again three parts;
the first clarifies the essence of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Second, the explanation of the characteristics of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Third, the summary of the characteristics of the lineage by concluding that the spiritual lineages possessed by all bodhisattvas are associated with such qualities as these.
Within the second section, there are further four parts.
First, the essence of the two kinds of spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is clarified;
second, their names are explained;
third, they are distinguished as coarse or subtle in relation to their respective fruits.
Fourth, distinguishing the superiority of advancement over inferiority.
This provides a brief clarification of the meaning of the two lineages (gotra) through five gates.
First, the discernment of their essence.
Regarding the three explanations from the West:
according to the teaching of Jayasena,
there is no distinct essence to the lineage or spiritual family (gotra).
However, within that body, there is the sense that the two kinds of obstacles can be severed.
Thus, one establishes oneself in the original family and abides in the lineage;
subsequently, encountering a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), hearing the Dharma, and generating the resolve to seek enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
Prior to the stages of the Path (bhūmi), there are four types of permeation resulting from hearing.
First, from the category of merit (puṇyabhāga), one gradually cultivates and perfects the out-flowing wholesome states;
as these states of the Path (mārgabhāga) are gradually cultivated and increased, they permeate and form uncontaminated seeds (anāsravabīja).
This is called the lineage of the stage of practice (*śikṣāgotra*). It refers to the arising of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and so forth.
This is established according to the system of Ratnamati.
There exists, by nature and from the beginning, the untainted seed as one's lineage (gotra).
Subsequently, upon hearing the Dharma during the stage of the ten faiths, one arouses the mind;
this then nurtures and brings forth the original seeds from the manifest mind, causing them to increase and become preeminent.
This is called the lineage of cultivation (*abhyāsa-gotra*).
From the perspective of its inherent existence, it is termed the "lineage of nature" (*prakṛti-gotra*);
by virtue of its increase through cultivation, it is termed the "lineage of cultivation."
It is clarified that at a later time, no new seeds are further perfumed;
rather, based on the principle of the single essence of the old seeds, it is taught that even prior to the stages (bhūmi), there are two types of lineage (*gotra*).
This is according to the system of Dharmapāla.

Although prior to the stages of the path (bhūmi), those impure (sāsrava) perfumations by hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) serve as the resources that increase the fundamental seeds— just as the sprouts of ginger, for instance, are of the same nature as their original substance—
they nonetheless belong to the category of what is innately present (*sahaja*). Thus, they are collectively subsumed under the lineage (*gotra*) residing within the innate nature.
Thus, prior to the stages (bhūmi), there is no essence of the untainted lineage-seed;
rather, it arises solely from the lineage-nature.
At the first moment of the first stage, there is non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna).
Once this wisdom has arisen, it immediately perfumes and forms seeds; these are the essence of the untainted lineage of practice (*anāsrava-śikṣā-gotra*).
As for the tainted lineage of practice (*sāsrava-śikṣā-gotra*), it exists prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
Second is the naming:
what was formerly called the "nature-lineage" (prakṛti-gotra) is now called the "naturally abiding lineage" (prakṛtistha-gotra).
The former was called the "nature of the lineage of practice" (śikṣāgotra), while the present is called the "nature accomplished through practice" (śikṣāniṣpannagotra).
Within this context, these two types of lineage share a common designation.
The name is established by proceeding from the enumeration to the meaning.
Regarding the specific names "nature" (*prakṛti*) and "cultivation" (*vāsanā*): the "nature-seed" (*prakṛtisthagotra*) receives its name based on its own essential substance.
The "nature of the stage of practice" (*śikṣāgotra*) is named after its skillful means (*upāya*).
Thirdly, it is distinguished according to the sequence of stages. Jing says:
According to Ratnacandra,
the meaning of the innate nature-seed being primordially present resides in the initial stage of the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*),
wherein the perfuming of the supporting conditions causes that nature-seed to increase.
This is precisely what is called the "cultivated nature" (*śikṣā-bīja*). There is no separate substantial entity for this cultivated nature;
from the stage of the ten faiths onward, it coexists eternally with the two natures.
Even after entering the first bhūmi and beyond, seeds are not perfumed.
As the treatise states regarding "perfuming":
it is merely the act of perfuming and activating pre-existing seeds that is called "perfuming seeds."
According to Dharmapāla,
it is said that from the stage prior to the ten faiths up through the forty mental states of the stage before the path of seeing constitutes the lineage (*gotra*).
Although, while prior to the stages [of the path], the function of the innate seeds is increased through the stimulation of the perfuming of hearing— which is still of a contaminated nature—
it remains of the same category as that which is innately possessed;
therefore, it is classified as being subsumed within the lineage-seeds (*gotra-bīja*).

Because prior to the stage of the path (bhūmi), there have been no manifest outflow-free states (*anāsrava*) to separately perfuse and form seeds, there is no outflow-free lineage of habitual seeds (*vāsanā-gotra*).
Therefore, prior to that stage, the lineage consists only of the seeds of hearing-perfuming (*śruta-vāsanā*) which are still with-outflow; this is what is termed the "lineage of habitual seeds."
Once one has entered the stages (*bhūmi*), the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) manifestations perfume and form seeds; thus, there exists the substance of the outflow-free lineage (*gotra*).
The meaning of this will be addressed later, where Woncheuk provides a distinct interpretation.
The textual analysis shall be presented below.
Master Ce’s commentary explains that there are three meanings. First:

This treatise is structured according to the sequence of origin and culmination: the nature-lineage (prakṛtisthagotra) is presented first, and the developmental lineage (samudānītagotra) follows as the latter.
Second is the analysis of the factors of sustenance (*pariṣkāra*).
Because they mutually sustain one another,
their sequence is not fixed.
This means that by the nature of things (dharmatā), there is habitual cultivation;
by virtue of this habitual cultivation, growth is attained.
This is the third point, discussed according to the actual reality.
There is no sequence of before or after;
this is because from the stage of the ten faiths upward, up to the diamond-like samādhi, there exist two lineages.
Fourth is the penetration or obstruction of conditions.
The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla says:
When two different natures are compared, there exists only the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*);
because they are not of the same nature, there is no causal condition (*hetupratyaya*).
Because the seed-dharma does not take an object as its condition, it lacks an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
It also lacks an immediate-condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), because it is a seed.
In terms of its nature, it is expected that at the first stage (bhūmi), there arises non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
This has causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), augmenting conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), object conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and sequential conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
When two lineages are compared in relation to subsequently attained wisdom,
there are three conditions but no immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
because these two lineages are compared in relation to the manifestation of the Buddha-fruit.
It possesses three conditions,
excluding the condition of immediate succession (*samanantarapratyaya*). Thus says the Master Rāmaśrībhadra.
Because the two natures are mutually identical in essence, there are no four conditions [between them].
When the nature-seed-nature (prakṛtisthagotra) is compared to the fundamental wisdom (mūlaprajñā) of the first stage, there are two conditions;
when compared to the subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna), there are three conditions.
This can be understood.
Jayasena states that the nature-lineage (prakṛtisthagotra) has no substantial entity.
Therefore, it is not discussed here.

Regarding the relationship between the stage of the lineage through practice (*śikṣāgotra*) and the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) of the first bhūmi, there are two interpretations. One says:
There is a causal condition. Why is this?
Because they are equally the Truth of the Path.
One school says:
there is only the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*),
just as, for example, the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkhadharmakṣānti*) in the Hīnayāna has no homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*).
Fifth, the classification according to the fruit of Buddhahood:
according to the meaning of Dharmapāla, the nature-seed-lineage (*prakṛti-gotra*) is the direct cause and condition for the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*),
but it is not the direct cause and condition for the other two bodies.
If one considers the eight consciousnesses and the four wisdoms, they constitute the direct causes and conditions.
Regarding the seeds of the lineage (*gotra*) as they relate to the three bodies (*trikāya*), they possess two conditions, namely:
the causal condition and the dominant condition.
Regarding the eight consciousnesses and the four wisdoms, there are two interpretations. One says:
from the first bhūmi upward, there are the wisdom of the fundamental nature (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).
Because it perfumes and forms the seeds of habituation, the fruit of Buddhahood arises.
In relation to the two wisdoms, and in relation to the sixth and seventh consciousnesses,
they can function as three conditions, excluding the sequential condition.

It is said that the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and the Wisdom of Accomplishing What is to be Done have only two conditions, namely, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
One school asserts this.

Regarding the seeds of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) and the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) in relation to the four wisdoms and the eight consciousnesses, they possess three conditions,
excluding the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). Thus says Dharmaruci.
Regarding the principle that the two natures are of one substance yet distinct in meaning:
when viewed in relation to the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), the eight consciousnesses and the four wisdoms all possess the three conditions.
Excluding the condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Śūra states:
"Because the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*) and the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) infuse and form seeds."
It is capable of producing the eight consciousnesses and four wisdoms of the Buddha-fruit.
The text states:

"That is to say, the six bases of the Bodhisattvas possess such characteristics, having been transmitted successively from beginningless time, obtained through the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)," and so forth.
"Jingyun" (Scenic Clouds) refers to those bodhisattvas who are individuals of the Mahāyāna lineage.
Regarding the excellence of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana-viśeṣa*):
according to the traditional interpretation,
this refers to the Buddha-nature abiding in its own nature (*prakṛtistha-gotra*), which is the *tathāgatagarbha*.
There are inconceivable merits, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, which are inseparable, non-detached, and non-different;
because these are now fully possessed as the merits of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*),
it is said that the six sense bases are preeminent.
Now it is not so. As for the "six bases," these are simply the six bases, such as the eye and so forth.
Regarding the term "preeminent":
the ālayavijñāna is the sense base of mind (manāyatana),
and it is the most preeminent among the six sense bases.
The sublime mental sphere (manāyatana) is the basis for the lineage of the nature (prakṛtigateya);
thus it is said that it possesses such characteristics.
This collectively reveals the substance of the nature-seed (prakṛti-bīja) that serves as the basis for the dependent [qualities].
Because this Mahāyāna nature-seed has existed from the very beginning,
it is said to exist "from time without beginning."
Its essence is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
for it has continued up to the present through the succession of the ālayavijñāna;
it leads to and transmits [the seeds] from one to another.
Because it is not produced through perfuming,
it is said to be "attained through the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*). Furthermore, another interpretation is as follows:
The essence of the nature-lineage (prakṛtisthagotra) generally relies upon the internal six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) of a bodhisattva; therefore,
it is called the "six bases."
Even so, it also depends upon the body of the six external sense bases;
however, it is not a sentient being.
Because this [distinction] is not fixed,
it speaks only of the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātmikāyatana*).
As for what is called "preeminent":
This explains the essential nature of the lineage of those destined for correctness (*samyaktva-niyata-gotra*). The characteristics described below are analyzed in detail;
this analysis is as previously stated.
This [explanation] is based on the Tripiṭaka and constitutes these two interpretations.
Furthermore, there are others who interpret it as follows:
although it universally relies upon the six internal and external bases (āyatana), it does not exceed the number six.
It simply mentions the six sense bases;
the remaining meanings are as explained previously.
Regarding the "cultivated lineage" (śikṣā-gotra):
According to Jayasena,
one first gradually cultivates the roots of goodness belonging to the category of merit (*puṇyabhāgīya*) until they become the category of the path (*mārgabhāgīya*);
by practicing these successively, one eventually perfumes them into uncontaminated seeds (*anāsravabīja*).
This is called the nature of the stage of cultivation. According to Ratnamati,
the nature of the lineage is inherently existent.

Subsequently, upon entering the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), one hears the Dharma and generates the aspiration for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*); this serves as the nourishing influence that causes the originally existing nature-seed (*prakṛti-bīja*) to increase.
This is called the "nature of the cultivated seed" (*śikṣita-bīja-gotra*). According to Dharmapāla:
The nature-seed (prakṛtisthagotra) increases through its own kind of supportive flow and is thus merely called the "nature-seed.
The outflowing uncontaminated (anāsrava) states, however, perfuse [the mind] specifically to form the seeds of the spiritual lineage (gotra).
Therefore, it is called the "cultivated seed" (*śikṣā-bīja*).
This refers to that which is obtained through the prior cultivation and habituation of roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*).
Tái (Tài) says:
Regarding the excellence of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*),
the Western masters present six explanations. One says:
It is attached to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*),
because the superior functional capacity of the untainted seeds (*anāsravabīja*) is subsumed within the six sense bases.
Second, it says:
There are seeds of the two obstructions attached to the six sense bases and subsumed within them.
Because these seeds of the two obstructions must necessarily be abandoned, they are termed "sublime.
These are the two aforementioned explanations.
According to the gate of conventional reasoning,
[it is so]; however, according to the gate of ultimate truth,
only the sixth sense-base contains uncontaminated seeds.
Alternatively, regarding the meaning that the two obstacles can be severed,
it is stated as "six bases" (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) by way of a general enumeration based on their major categories.
Thirdly, it says:
Among the six sense bases, there is a preeminent base,
namely the mind base (manāyatana).
Within the mind base, that which is preeminent is—
This refers to the sixth consciousness,
the mind; that which is preeminent within the sixth consciousness is the untainted seed.
Alternatively, the seeds of the two hindrances may be severed;
this refers to grasping them by way of their essential nature and their functioning.
As it says in the *Four [Treatises]*:
The eighth consciousness possesses both the objective (nimitta-bhāga) and subjective (darśana-bhāga) aspects.
The five bases, such as the eye, constitute the objective aspect;
the sixth base within this [eighth consciousness] is the subjective aspect of the ālayavijñāna.
These six sense bases are, in their entirety, the objective (nimitta-bhāga) and subjective (darśana-bhāga) aspects of the fundamental consciousness (mūla-vijñāna).
Within the self-substance aspect (svabhāva-bhāga), which serves as the basis for these objective and subjective aspects,
there exists the superior functional capacity of untainted seeds (anāsrava-bīja).
Alternatively, it refers to the capacity to sever the seeds of the two hindrances.
This citation illustrates the specific, superior capacities inherent within its essential nature.
As the *Pañcavastuka* states:
Within the eighth consciousness, there exist the superior functional capacities of the seeds of the six bases, such as the uncontaminated eye and so forth;
there are also the uncontaminated seeds of the six bases, such as form and so forth.
This is explained from the perspective of the predominant factor;
it simply mentions the six bases (ṣaḍāyatana) and does not mention the twelve bases (dvādaśāyatana).
Sixth, it is said:
"There truly exist the seeds of the twelve untainted bases (*anāsrava-āyatana*);
however, because they do not exceed six, only six are mentioned."
It is like the seven-leaf tree (*saptaparṇa*).
The masters of the West mostly maintain differing views;
they hold that the inherently existing untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) are what constitute their excellence.
Ji says: The fundamental lineage and the lineage of cultivated seeds are established according to the circumstances,
following the three meanings of "new" and "old" as appropriate.
Some say that it is not the case that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla takes the stages above the ground (bhūmi) as "cultivation" (*śikṣā*); for even before the grounds,
during the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), one gives rise to untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*).
When that seed is produced, it is called the "cultivated lineage" (*abhyāsa-gotra*).
It is described as "produced" because it increases accordingly.
This is the distinct interpretation of the master Saṃghabhadra.
According to Master Weishengjun, the "original lineage" (*prakṛti-gotra*) is established in terms of its functional capacity to sever the cognitive obstructions (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).
The "cultivated lineage" (*samudānīta-gotra*) refers to the seeds of contaminated hearing, reflection, and so forth, which are acquired during the stage of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Question: What is the arising of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)?
Explanation: There are two meanings.

The supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgradharma) serves as the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for the arising of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), this alone is untainted (*anāsrava*).
It does not arise from causes and conditions.
Alternatively, it may arise with the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*) as its cause and condition;
through long-term cultivation, the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) can be severed.
The most excellent among tainted wholesome states,
by virtue of its supreme nature, serves as the causal condition for the arising of the Dharma-patience regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti).
The intention of this master [Vasubandhu] is to employ [the preceding] as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*),
just as will be explained later;
whereas the doctrine established by the former masters [Dharmatrāta and others] is that it arises from the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
This is established because it accords with what has been transmitted since antiquity and because one wishes to distinguish a specific meaning.
Those whose intention is to ascend do so solely for the sake of protecting the meaning of the Dharma.
Some say that it is not the case that one has not yet distinguished the seeds at the stage of the ten faiths while protecting the Dharma; this is incorrect.
As stated in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, there are distinctions:
prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), there are three minds.
The first is the mind of faith (*śraddhā-citta*).
The second is the abiding mind;
the third is the firm mind.
Within the stage of faith, these are termed the "cultivated lineage" (*śikṣamāṇagotra*).
"Abiding" refers to the ten stages of understanding (*adhimukti*) and the ten stages of practice (*caryā*), which together constitute the stage of abiding (*vihāra*).
"Firm resolve" refers to the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
I have searched for that scripture in the West but have not yet heard of an extant copy.
Nevertheless, let us now synthesize this for the moment.
According to the intent of that sūtra, the lineage (*gotra*) is generally described as comprising many types of lineages.
Thus, that very sūtra speaks of the "lineage of practice" (*śikṣā-gotra*).
This refers to being in the stage of faith, which is the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).
As for the "nature-lineage" (*prakṛti-gotra*),
it refers to being in the stage of abiding in the mind.
Abiding in the mind within that sutra refers precisely to the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*) and the ten stages of practice (*daśa-caryā*).
These ten understandings and ten practices are termed the "nature-lineage" (*prakṛti-gotra*). Question:
Why does that sutra first clarify the "cultivated lineage" (gotra) and subsequently clarify the "original lineage"?
The commentary states:
"At the time of initial cultivation, it is called the 'cultivated lineage'."
When subsequent practice has become established as a nature, it is called the "nature-lineage" (*prakṛti-gotra*).
Therefore, this sequence of prior and subsequent [stages] does not accord with the meaning of this treatise.
Question: For what reason are those twenty minds combined into ten abidings?
Does the *Avataṃsaka* and other scriptures open with twenty minds?
The commentary states: This is for the purpose of distinguishing between the preceding and succeeding stages.
Because it was previously generated through the arising of predominant faith,
it is distinguished from what preceded it;
furthermore, since it does not immediately follow the initial path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is distinct.
Therefore, although twenty mental states are combined, they are designated as a single dwelling.
Thus, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* refers to the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*) as the "lineage of the path" (*mārga-gotra*),
because they are proximate to the path of seeing and the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).

To claim that what follows the path of seeing (darśanamārga) is called the "lineage of practice" (caryagotra) is not logically tenable, whether according to the intent of that sūtra or the intent of this treatise,
because their lineages (gotra) are distinct.
Regarding the statement that "in this context, both the meaning and the phrasing are accepted":
if one follows the older *Bhūmisaṃgraha*, this passage does not exist;
however, the Tripitaka Master has now fully provided this text based on the Sanskrit original.
Now, summarizing both natures as the lineage-holders (*gotra-dhara*),
it is said that "both types are taken.
This is within the section explaining the different names.
The two kinds of lineage (gotra) are called "seeds" (bīja) because they can produce fruits;
they are called "elements" (dhātu) because they can sustain fruits;
and they are called "lineage" (gotra) because they are the nature and category of qualities as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
In the section distinguishing the coarse and the subtle,
the *Dìchí jīng* (Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra) states:
"Furthermore, for those who do not practice, the fruit is subtle and the fruit is distant."
For those who practice, the fruit is coarse and the fruit is near.
As an ancient said:
"The nature-seed is unconditioned and is not a dharma of cultivation."
Therefore, it is said that they are not practiced;
because names are abandoned and signs are severed,
it is said that the fruit is subtle.
It cannot be fathomed by ordinary sentiment;
therefore, it is said that its fruition is remote.
Because the seeds of practice (*śikṣā-bīja*) are conditioned phenomena that can be cultivated, they are termed "practice" (*śikṣā*).
Because they possess names and characteristics, the fruits they lead toward are coarse;
because they can be conceived by the intellect, the fruits are said to be near.
Some say that because the previously existing seeds of habituation are able to realize them, they are called "coarse" and "near."
That which is later realized as the nature-seed (*prakṛti-gotra*) is called "subtle" and "distant.
The current translation differs entirely from the old one;
the meaning of the text explains this solely in terms of the nature-seed lineage (*prakṛti-gotra*).
The Tripiṭaka Master says:
Furthermore, as for this lineage (gotra) which has not yet practiced to fruition and is called "subtle," it means that the fruit of the lineage which has not yet been practiced is called "subtle."
If the fruit of the lineage of practice (*śikṣāgotra*) is attained, it is then termed "coarse.

The reason for this is that from the moment the resolve [for awakening] is generated onward, because of the lineage of practice, [the qualities] gradually increase and become increasingly clear; therefore, it is called "coarse."
Master Ji says: According to the interpretation of Vijayasena and others,
that which has not yet generated the bodhicitta and has not yet cultivated the fruit of the spiritual lineage (gotra) is called "subtle."
Because the fruit of the lineage of cultivation has not yet arisen;
whereas from the moment the mind is first generated onward, since there is already the fruit of cultivation,
it is said to be "coarse" because it functions simultaneously with the fruit of the lineage of cultivation.
Within the interpretation of Candrapāla, there are also two explanations.
One interpretation holds that the innate lineage (prakṛti-gotra) has not yet been formed through cultivation.
When the outflowing (sāsrava) activity of the stage prior to the ground is manifesting, it is called "subtle";
when it has become an outflowing fruit, it is called "coarse," because it coexists with the present mind.
This is because it serves as the innate, untainted dominant condition for the fruit of generating the bodhicitta;
this is the second explanation.
Before the stages (*bhūmi*), the two types—the lineage (*gotra*) and the habitual (*vāsanā*)—have not yet been fully cultivated and perfected.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, the fruit of the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) is called "subtle";
only when the untainted mind is fully established is it termed "coarse."
Because it coexists with the fruit of the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*),
there are also two explanations regarding the meaning of "protecting the Dharma" (*dharmasaṃrakṣaṇa*).
One explanation states:
When the nature of the stage of cultivation has not yet been perfected through practice,
the seeds newly produced at the time of their fruition are called "subtle.
If they have already been perfected through practice, the seeds newly produced at the time of their fruition are called "coarse."
One interpretation holds that because it is conjoined with a new type of fruit (*phala*),
its meaning is identical to the latter interpretation of Rāma.
Master Ji said:

"This refers to the initial stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), where the permeated untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) increase and multiply; therefore, it is described in terms of 'coarse' and 'subtle,' rather than referring to other stages."
What is meant by "simultaneous"?
It refers to the principle of protecting [the dharma],
which further establishes a distinct seed.
Both the newly arisen seed and the ancient seed may be explained in this manner,
according to the interpretation of Candragupta.
It is simply that when the old [seed] increases, it is explained as a "fruit" in the sense of being a newly increased seed within the continuum of thought;
the previously existing seed is explained as the "cause.
Therefore, they are said to be simultaneous.
Furthermore, when considering a preceding moment in relation to a succeeding moment,
although they are distinct and there is the cessation of the cause and the arising of the effect across different instants,
it is precisely because the cause exists that it is able to produce its effect.
Therefore, it is said that they are "together," as in the sense of Vijitāvin.
The seeds of beginningless, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) wholesome dharmas are called the cause.
At the initial stage of the ten faiths, the untainted teachings (anāsrava-śāsana) perfuming the causal conditions produce new seeds;
these seeds are the fruit,
while the seeds from time immemorial serve as the cause.
Because cause and effect are simultaneous, they are said to be "co-existent" (*sahabhū*).
In distinguishing the superior from the inferior, first there is a brief explanation followed by a detailed one.
As for the statement, "If all bodhisattvas... up to the unsurpassed and most excellent," [it refers to this].
It is said: "This merely constitutes the cause for the lineage of the Mahāyāna;
it has already transcended the fruit of the Two Vehicles."
How much more so for all sentient beings who lack such a nature?
According to the masters of the *Awakening of Faith*,

it is said that when the afflictions of all sentient beings arise, they are simultaneously imbued with the nature of untainted liberation, whereby all things are perfumed to form the lineage of the Mahāyāna.

In that case, there would be no distinction between the superiority and inferiority of the three vehicles, nor would there be any differentiation between those with the nature [for enlightenment] and those without it.
How, then, can one accord with this passage?
Even before generating the resolve for enlightenment, one who merely possesses the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) already surpasses those of the two vehicles,
let alone all others who lack the lineage.
As Ji says:
Those who have attained the lineage of a bodhisattva prior to the ten stages of faith already surpass the śaikṣas and aśaikṣas of the two vehicles,
let alone all other ordinary beings.
Why is this? All sentient beings possess two kinds of obstructions.
Nevertheless, from time immemorial prior to the seven stages of expedient means, they have established the seeds of the two vehicles.
Because the afflictive hindrance (kleśāvaraṇa) can be severed,
one will only be able to realize the purification of the afflictive hindrance;
however, the cognitive hindrance (jñeyāvaraṇa) is ultimately incapable of being severed.
It is not possible to realize the purification of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) directly;
however, the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) vary in degree— being either heavy or light—
because of the differences in the sharpness or dullness of one's faculties.
There is a distinction between the two vehicles.
If one has established the lineage of a bodhisattva,
this has been so since beginningless time, prior to the stage of the ten faiths.
Because the two obstacles are certain to be severed,
it is the unsurpassed excellence when compared to those four types.

Thus, within the realm of *tathatā* (suchness) that constitutes the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), the five lineages (*gotra*) are established based on whether there are obstructions or no obstructions;
in meaning, there is no difference,
as will be understood from that [text].
Now, I shall resolve Master Jing’s doubts:
the *Awakening of Faith* relies on the principle that the inconceivable perfuming of True Suchness (*tathatā*) receives perfuming,
whereas the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* relies on the principle that the conceivable perfuming of the ālayavijñāna receives perfuming.
The Dharma-gates are each distinct and cannot be standardized by a single measure. Why is this?
The following questions and answers provide a detailed explanation.
The intent of the question is this:
Since the three vehicles equally sit upon the bed of liberation,
why is it that those of the bodhisattva lineage surpass those of the two vehicles even while still among ordinary beings?
The answer consists of two parts:
first, explaining the smallness of the fault by means of the exhaustion of both obstacles;
second, explaining the smallness of the fault by means of four matters.
Regarding the two obstacles,
a brief analysis of their essential nature reveals four levels.
First, the analysis of their nature according to five levels.

Furthermore, the four abodes of existence (*catur-vāsabhūmi*) constitute the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*), while the abode of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) constitutes the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
These two are categorized in terms of the two types of grasping: grasping at persons and grasping at phenomena.
The Tripitaka Master says:
"Only the view of self is considered a human-grasping (pudgala-grāha);
all other external afflictions are not human-graspings."
If one takes "clinging to categories" as the basis for the general designation "clinging to persons," there is no error in the meaning. Furthermore,
regarding the relationship between clinging to phenomena (*dharman-grāha*) and the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), there are two interpretations.
One explanation says:
the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is broad while the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is narrow.
The reason for this is as follows:
Because within phenomena there is no such thing as ignorance that clings to them as being non-dharmas.
One interpretation states:
the clinging to dharmas (dharmagrāha) and the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) are equal in their scope, neither being broader nor narrower than the other.
The intention of the Tripiṭaka masters is that the later interpretation is superior.
This is because they distinguish [the afflictions] based on the seven consciousnesses:

the five sensory consciousnesses give rise only to the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), as they are direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*) and thus do not constitute the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The two obstacles arise simultaneously with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
whereas the manas is not fixed.
One interpretation holds that the manas possesses only the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The Tripitaka Master said:
"If the manas did not possess the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) consisting of attachment to dharmas,
there would be a great deal of contradiction."
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the ālayavijñāna, even in its most minimal state, must necessarily function simultaneously with at least one other consciousness.

This is as in the case of those of the Two Vehicles—whether they be learners (*śaikṣa*) or non-learners (*aśaikṣa*)—who have entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and lack the manas.
At that time, the ālayavijñāna exists as a solitary consciousness alone; it cannot be said that even the minimum of two consciousnesses function simultaneously.
Furthermore, the seventy-eighth [fascicle] states:
"From the eighth stage onward, all afflictions no longer manifest."
It takes only the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as its basis.
When the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of those in the eighth stage and above enters the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*),
the manas immediately gives rise to attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), which is termed the cognitive obscuration.
Therefore, both the sixth and seventh consciousnesses give rise to the two obstacles.
Regarding the fourfold classification according to the three natures,
as for the obstacle of afflictions:
These are exclusively unwholesome and obscured-neutral states.
Regarding the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
there are three differing interpretations in the Western lands (India).
One says it is exclusively defiled;
another says...
It is common to both [the wholesome and unwholesome] natures. One school says it is common to all three natures.
The intention of the Tripiṭaka masters lies in [classifying it as] two natures, excluding the wholesome;
the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that it mostly retains the grasping at dharmas (*dharmagrāha*),
