which is of the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), fascicle nine, states that [the path] applies to both natures.
Next, regarding the clarification of the abandonment of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
if it pertains to those abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*):
They are abandoned in the first bhūmi.
Regarding those to be abandoned through cultivation, there are three grades;
the upper and middle grades have already been suppressed in the first bhūmi.
Ultimately, they do not function [as such],
because even up through the seventh stage, inferior-grade afflictions still arise.
As the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
If the manas-vijñāna did not exist in the fifth, sixth, and seventh stages,
the afflictions of the six consciousnesses would not be able to arise;
from the eighth stage onward, even the inferior grade [of afflictions] is suppressed.
The "Chapter on Abiding in the Lower [Stages]" states that there are two obstacles and three points of error:
first, the heavy latencies (*dausthulya*) of afflictions in the evil destinies are abandoned at the time of the first stage;
second, the heavy latencies of afflictions associated with the obstacle of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) are abandoned at the eighth stage.
Regarding the third point—the severance of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) in the tenth stage:
according to the principle of cultivation-based severance, the afflictions are severed all at once in a single moment upon reaching the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*).
As for the statement that [afflictions] are abandoned in the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*),
this is based on the fact that they are permanently suppressed and do not manifest upon reaching the eighth stage; thus,
their suppression is described as "abandonment."
Among the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
those that are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) are abandoned in the first stage (*bhūmi*).
If it is abandoned through cultivation,
it is gradually severed moment by moment from the second stage onward, reaching total exhaustion only at the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
However, within the section on the "stages of abiding" (*vihāra*), the third fault regarding the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is discussed.
This means that "the abandonment by the Bodhisattva dwelling in the supreme fulfillment" refers to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Regarding the third fault among the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
"the abandonment by the Tathāgata dwelling [in the state]" refers to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
This is the *Chāyā-saṃkṣepa-dharmaparyāya*.

Regarding the statement that those belonging to the lineage of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are only able to realize the purification of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇaviśuddhi*) and so forth:
one asks, "Why was it stated in the previously established thesis that the bodhisattva lineage surpasses all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others?"
In the subsequent commentary, it states that those of the śrāvaka lineage and so forth realize only the purification of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
whereas those of the bodhisattva lineage shall realize the purification of both obstructions.
This passage, therefore, explains the causes for transcending the two vehicles.
Why are the preceding and succeeding [sections] contradictory?
The explanation says:
there is no harm in this, as it is a concise presentation where each part illuminates the other.
Furthermore, one may cite the lineage to clarify the fruit,
rather than wishing to clarify the lineage itself among the four superior matters.
Regarding the excellence of practice, there are two distinct types of beneficial conduct for bodhisattvas:
causing others to obtain the causes of mundane goodness is called "benefit" (hita),
and causing them to obtain the fruits of mundane goodness is called "well-being" (sukha).
Furthermore, causing one to obtain the fruit of future happiness is called "benefit" (hita),
while causing one to obtain present happiness is called "well-being" (sukha).
As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
Causing [beings] to attain supramundane happiness is called "benefit" (hita);
causing them to attain mundane happiness is called "well-being" (sukha).
Here, both mundane benefit and well-being are explained in general.
This applies to all five destinies.
Regarding the statement that, out of compassion, he commands those humans and devas to protect [the teaching] so that they may attain the supreme truth (*paramārtha*),
this is because the faculties of the human and celestial paths are capable of receiving the supramundane, untainted (*anāsrava*) supreme truth.
Among the skillful excellences (*kauśalya-viśeṣa*),
only five types are explained here; in other places,
the afflictions (*kleśa*) are further added, either as the truths (*satya*) or as the bases (*āyatana*).
It clarifies the seven additional faculties and so forth.
Those of the two vehicles possess analytical skill only regarding the aggregates, elements, bases, dependent origination, and the possible and impossible;
they are unable to achieve mastery through thorough penetration of the five fields of knowledge and so forth.
The bodhisattva is not like that;
he attains skillfulness in all respects and is therefore superior in his skillfulness compared to those of the two vehicles.
In the second section, which clarifies the characteristics of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*),
the text is divided into three parts.
First, the essential framework is briefly presented.
Next, there is the detailed explanation according to specific categories, followed by the summary.
Regarding the former, Jing says:
The untainted seeds that exist by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) constitute the essence of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Based on these seeds, one practices the six perfections;
this manifestation of a bodhisattva possessing the essence of the spiritual lineage is termed the "characteristic of the spiritual lineage" (*gotra-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the essential nature of the six perfections:

the perfection of giving—both the gift of Dharma and the gift of material wealth—has as its essence the volitional action associated with the wholesome root of non-attachment, together with the bodily and vocal actions it initiates, and the five aggregates that arise simultaneously with them.
The gift of fearlessness has as its essence the five aggregates, such as volition, which are associated with the wholesome root of non-aversion.
According to the meaning of *dāna* (giving), it is subsumed within the six perfections.
Thus, it takes as its essence all wholesome dharmas produced by the three types of action (karman) arising from the three roots of goodness.
Regarding the three aggregates of giving and morality,
they likewise take all wholesome dharmas as their essence.
Among the types of patience (*kṣānti*), the patience regarding harm from others has non-aversion (*adveṣa*) as its essence.
Regarding the patience in accepting suffering, the Tripiṭaka masters state that its nature is diligence (*vīrya*).
Alternatively, since one is able to endure through the application of wisdom (*jñāna*), it may also be considered that its nature is wisdom.
Dharma-patience (dharma-kṣānti) has the nature of the patience of reflection and the patience of liberation,
and its substance consists of the five aggregates arising simultaneously.
Diligence (vīrya), as a distinct nature, has the mental factors of meditative concentration (dhyāna) and diligence as its substance.
If one takes the three types of karma that arise simultaneously [with the mind], then all five aggregates are diligence (*vīrya*).
Meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) takes as its essence the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) among the specific mental objects;
all dharmas of merit produced by means of concentration are likewise termed meditative concentration.
The function of wisdom (prajñā) takes as its essence the mental factor of wisdom among the specific objects of cognition (viśeṣālambana).
Among the ten pāramitās, the latter four are conventional wisdoms (saṃvṛti-jñāna), while the sixth,
prajñāpāramitā, is the wisdom that takes ultimate reality (tattva) as its object.
If only the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) were established,
then the sixth would encompass both the ultimate and conventional truths. Tái said:
Although the acts of giving and so forth performed since beginningless time are not themselves the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*),
they possess the characteristics of that perfection; by means of these characteristics,
others can infer that the true bodhisattva lineage actually exists within their bodies.
According to the detailed explanation in the text, there are six sections.
Within the section on discerning giving (*dāna*), there are three parts.
First is the inquiry that initiates the discussion.
Next is the formal explanation;
third is the summary.
Within the formal explanation:
First, the three types of giving are distinguished;
second, they are analyzed through six phrases.
Within the former, there are again two parts.
The first clarifies that the bodhisattva’s fundamental nature delights in giving;
the second concerns the ability to practice toward specific objects.
This ability to practice is further divided into three parts.
First, the giving of material wealth is clarified;
next, the giving of the Dharma is distinguished;
finally, the giving of fearlessness.

In the section on the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*), the first part clarifies the practice of giving toward the field of compassion (*karuṇākṣetra*), while the latter part clarifies the practice of giving toward the field of reverence (*gurukṣetra*). Within the practice of compassionate giving,
the initial portion clarifies giving when one possesses material wealth.
The latter clarifies the giving of non-material things (*adhana-dāna*).
Within the category of material giving, the former clarifies the giving of abundant wealth;
although the material goods may be few, the latter clarifies the giving of meager wealth (*parītta-dāna*).
Among the various forms of giving material wealth, there are three moments of purity of mind:
joy before the gift, and gladness during the actual act of giving.
Having given, one has no regrets.
Whether the object is abundant, one gives universally; whether it is meager, one aids the poor.
One’s words are free from stinginess, and when practicing deep-seated shame regarding what one has not yet given, one praises the act of giving for others.
This is the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*).
The field of respect (*gurukṣetra*) is easily understood.
Next, the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*) will be explained.
Regarding the phrase "in this world and in other worlds, etc.":
it means that throughout those three times, one acts as an uninvited friend in matters of abandoning evil and performing good deeds, constantly speaking with a compassionate heart.
The following clarifies the gift of fearlessness.
If sentient beings are terrified by kings or thieves,
this constitutes a hardship for those sentient beings.
Regarding "water, fire, and so forth," this is a challenge concerning insentient things (*nirjīva*).
The following six phrases provide a detailed analysis.
Regarding the phrase "having received another's property, never failing in one's duty," the first [part] indicates the presence of faith;
regarding the phrase "in relation to shared wealth," the second [part] indicates the presence of the sense of propriety.
Regarding the various mani-jewels, the third section below clarifies their uprightness;
the *Dìchí jīng* (Bhūmivastu-sūtra) explains this as non-greed,
though the phrasing and characteristics there differ entirely.
Jizang says:
The meaning here is that because people possess various kinds of rare treasures, their minds become deluded and inverted;
thus, they are unable to collect them and unable to guard them.
Because their minds were deluded when they previously entrusted it to others for safekeeping, they were unable to remember it;
yet the Bodhisattva was able to correctly awaken them so that he would never allow himself to be deceived or ensnared by them,
much less do so himself.
"His nature delights in vast wealth and status"—the fourth section below clarifies the vastness of his nature.
Ji says: "This means that because the Bodhisattva’s mind is vast."
Their minds delight in enjoyment;
it is not through meager wealth and status that their nature finds pleasure, but rather they delight in vast wealth and status.
This is because their activity is vast rather than narrow.

if one were to oppose only the obstacle to self-benefit and practice solely the conduct of self-benefit, it would indeed be merely self-benefit.
Self-benefit is an obstacle for a bodhisattva and is therefore not practiced;
now, to clarify that [the bodhisattva] acts solely for the sake of benefiting others,

if one considers only the practice for one's own benefit, there are only hindrances to self-benefit;

Therefore, in the subsequent explanation of benefiting others and benefiting both oneself and others, it says: "Furthermore, with the exception of the various explanations and characteristics mentioned previously, one should know that all other bodhisattva practices for benefiting others that are contrary to those [previously mentioned] are termed 'benefiting others and benefiting both oneself and others.'"
This is the reverse of the preceding: practicing generosity with wrong views;
and, holding the view that there is no cause or effect, preaching the Dharma to others while violating the precepts and departing from right conduct.
These two factors are obstacles solely to the benefit of others, whereas [the previous ones] were obstacles to benefiting both others and oneself.
This should also be understood as the reversal of purely altruistic obstacles into purely altruistic practice.
Now, to explain:
while the intention carries the sense of encompassing others, desire—though it reverses obstacles—applies to both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
The two preceding passages are similar.
Because a bodhisattva takes benefiting others as the fundamental principle,
only [actions] that benefit others, or those that benefit both self and others, do not constitute an obstruction.
If self-interest constitutes an obstacle,
then the three types of supernormal knowledge (vidyā) consist purely of benefiting others;
among these, there are two phrases that involve faults and should be abandoned.
First, the giving of material wealth accompanied by wrong views;
second, the giving of the Dharma by not believing in cause and effect and by disparaging the precepts.
Regarding the latter, there are three phrases that are faultless and should be practiced.

First, bodhisattvas who have already transcended the desire realm, out of the power of their compassion and vows, relinquish the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) for the sake of benefiting others and are reborn in the desire realm.
Second, bodhisattvas who have attained mastery manifest emanations (*nirmāṇa*) to benefit beings throughout the ten directions.
Third, the Buddhas, having fulfilled their own tasks, perform deeds for the benefit of others throughout the worlds of the ten directions by relying on their powers and fearlessnesses.

Regarding what has been explained above, the characteristics of what is to be abandoned and what is to be cultivated can be understood through this subsequent distinction between the correct and the incorrect.
The "two kinds" refers to the first two phrases.

"Furthermore, excluding the various characteristics previously mentioned," and so forth.
Jingyun: Excluding the aforementioned three phrases concerning those who abandon the various dhyānas for the sake of others and are reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
there are further other ways in which bodhisattvas should diligently train themselves and encourage others to act together for the benefit of others.
According to Master Gunaprabha’s statement:

excluding the aforementioned wrong views, the two practices of giving (*dāna*) and so forth that are obstacles solely to the benefit of others, those practices which are contrary to them and consist of benefiting others while also benefiting oneself are termed "shared with the benefit of others."
The second explanation, concerning benefit and happiness (*hitasukha*), is further divided into three parts:
first, a detailed explanation of the two characteristics of benefit and happiness;
second, a general discussion regarding the giving and non-giving of these two types.
The following summarizes it.
Within the preceding section, the characteristics of the benefits are first explained. Jizang says:
Regarding the types of benefit for oneself and others:
it is called a "type" because there is a single dharma that one practices oneself and causes others to practice, such that oneself and others perform this same single dharma.
Regarding the fourfold acceptance of dharmas: these refer to the four permutations consisting of happiness and suffering in this world and the next, which are termed the "acceptance of dharmas."
As determined below, four permutations are clarified by means of the wealthy and the poor, and those who observe and those who violate the precepts.
Question: In this context, the categories of benefit for oneself and others are being explained.
Why is it that the fourth dharma—the experience of suffering which is beneficial neither to this world nor the next—is also explained here?
Jizang says:
A bodhisattva does not accept the fourth dharma for the sake of benefiting themselves or others.
This is because if this practice were without benefit for oneself or others, the bodhisattva would have no intention to perform it.
Furthermore, by means of four dharmas, one receives instruction on self-benefit and knows what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced;
likewise, one instructs others and knows what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced.
Thus, both oneself and others know that what is to be practiced should be practiced and what is not to be practiced should not be practiced.
Therefore, both serve the purpose of benefiting [sentient beings].
Regarding the phrase "all nirvāṇa and the attainment of nirvāṇa, whether mundane or supramundane," within the fifth characteristic,
both nirvāṇa itself and the mundane and supramundane paths that attain nirvāṇa are collectively termed "quiescence" (śānti).
Ji says: "This refers back to the second and third matters previously mentioned; it is a general clarification that the first and fourth matters do not carry the intended meaning. Ce says:
Among these five characteristics, the first has as its essence the three types of action and the ten wholesome paths that are blameless and conducive to the benefit of oneself and others.

The second, "appropriation," has as its essence the uncontaminated, neutral, and resultant forms of pleasure, as well as the three feelings of joy, pleasure, and equanimity associated with the wholesome.
How is it known that the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is designated as "pleasure" (*sukha*) when it is not a transgression?
The subsequent text states: "The feeling of pleasure associated with outflows (*sāsrava-vedanā-sukha*) is bound to all three realms.
Therefore, we know that the feeling of equanimity is also called "pleasure."
This refers to the five sensory objects comprised within the various requisites, as well as the joy, bliss, and equanimity of meditative concentrations.
Regarding the phrase "happiness in this world and the next," it constitutes one portion of the four dharmas mentioned in the text concerning suffering in this world and happiness in future lives.
One takes up entirely the happiness of both worlds.
These two lines constitute the essence of the two types of karma.
Why is it that one does not take up happiness in this life at the expense of suffering in future lives?
To take the causes of suffering in future lives within the pleasures of this world is unwholesome;
therefore, one does not take them.
Alternatively, one may explain that among the pleasures of this world, there are also those that are wholesome or neutral.
Therefore, it also takes a small portion.
Regarding "the bliss of tranquility," this refers to nirvāṇa and the fivefold path consisting of the provisions for attaining nirvāṇa and so forth.
Question: Is the bliss that is free from fault identical to the bliss of appropriation?
Explanation: This is analyzed through a fourfold logical categorization (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There may be that which is blameless but not conducive;
namely, wholesome states associated with mental grief and physical pain.
There may also be that which is conducive but not blameless.
This refers to non-defiled pleasure and so forth, which are comprised within neutral offenses;
or it may be understood as possessing both phrases.
Or it may not be both types of pleasure.
With the exception of the aforementioned cases,
the remaining propositions should be understood accordingly.
Next, regarding the explanation of the characteristics of peace and happiness (*sukha*),
a brief presentation of the essential nature of the five types of happiness is as follows:
first, the happiness of the cause (*hetu-sukha*).
Baoliang says:
It has three factors as its essence;
namely, karma that accords with pleasant results, and the two factors of sense organs and objects which can produce contact conducive to pleasant feeling.
These three are the essence of cause and effect, which thus pervades the nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
This is because they universally include karma that accords with pleasant results.
As for the associated factors (*saṃprayukta*), if they exist, they all have pleasure as their essence and thus pervade the five aggregates as their substance.

Ce says: "The essence of cause and effect consists of the five faculties, six objects, and six contacts that accord with pleasant feeling, as well as the karma that brings about desirable fruits in both the present life and future lives.
He further explains:
"Manifesting as a present being" indicates the cause.

That is to say, the feeling of joy and pleasure (sukha-vedanā) takes both the tainted (sāsrava) and the untainted (anāsrava) as its substance.

This refers to joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). How is this known?

Master Ji says:
"The meditative concentration from the second dhyāna upward constitutes the very essence of this bliss."
Because it eliminates applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*),

This is the bliss of the four or three types of *sambodhi*.
Jizang says: "This refers to perfect enlightenment,
namely, the bliss of non-conceptual wisdom."
Alternatively, one may take the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) as the essence of this bliss.
This is because one attains this wisdom through the abandonment of afflictions,
and the bliss of the unconditioned nirvāṇa thus obtained is included within this bliss.
It is for the sake of realizing cessation that cessation is taught.
Since these are subsumed within the mind and mental factors, they constitute the essential nature of the five pleasures.

Therefore, one does not take up the bliss of the quiescence of nirvāṇa.
Ce (Cè) says:
Among the four kinds of bliss free from affliction and harm...
The first has morality as its essence;
the next two are concentration;
and the last is wisdom and abandonment.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and this treatise state:
"The two abandonments and the two knowledges are called bodhi.
Within this context, if one distinguishes them according to cause and effect:
Ce says: "The coarse aspect of discrimination [regarding] suffering and its antidote, pleasure, is only a cause and not a fruit;

Regarding its fruits, among the four types of happiness free from affliction and harm, the first three are causes and the last one is the fruit.
According to a detailed analysis, even the happiness that serves as an antidote to suffering can be categorized as both cause and fruit.

By assuming the bodies of great fish and so forth through emanation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), one pacifies the afflictions of sentient beings such as the suffering of hunger; this constitutes the "antidote" and so forth.
Therefore, it pertains to the fruit of Buddhahood.
As for the first three—freedom from affliction, non-harming, and bliss—they also pertain to both cause and fruit in terms of their ultimate reality.

The remaining three [types of bliss] pertain to both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). To analyze them in detail:
the bliss that is the antidote to suffering also pertains to the outflow-free, as it extends even to the fruit of Buddhahood.
Regarding the statement in the text, "The causes for pleasure refer to the two categories of pleasure," Jing says:
"There are two meanings regarding the 'outflow-free' (anāsrava)."
Alternatively, there are both bodily and mental pleasures.
Below, the causes of pleasure are set forth:
the sense faculties and their objects, when acting as causes for contact conducive to pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanīya-sparśa*), as well as karma that results in desirable and pleasant fruits.
The four dharmas serve as the cause.
Ji (基) says: "Regarding this statement 'caused by pleasure'..."
That which is the cause of pleasure is itself the cause of pleasure;
that is to say, the two factors of the sense faculty and the object are able to produce pleasant feeling,
and are therefore called the "two factors."
These are the causes of pleasure.
Furthermore, the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) can also give rise to contact conducive to painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanīyasparśa*);
here, we take those faculties and objects that give rise to contact conducive to pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanīyasparśa*).
The phrase "those whose faculties and objects exist within the state of pleasant feeling" refers to the category of the pleasant.
Furthermore, it is explained that there are two categories of the pleasant.
That is to say, the two types of pleasure within the nature of pleasure itself are the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, there are the two types of pleasure pertaining to body and mind.

In the present text, it is stated that the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) act as causes capable of producing these two kinds of pleasure—tainted and untainted—pertaining to both body and mind.
The faculties and objects are not treated as two separate entities, but rather as causes;
"intention" (manas) refers to the resulting fruit produced by them.
That is to say, the outflowing and non-outflowing sensations of pleasure and grasping take the productive causes—the faculties and objects—as their cause of pleasure.

Furthermore, regarding the two categories of pleasure (*sukha-pakṣa*), as previously mentioned, they take the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) fruits of body, mind, and so forth; both together take the two—the cause (the faculties) and the object—as the two categories of pleasure.
Although the fruit-pleasure is cited, the intention is to include causal pleasure.
Regarding the statement "experiencing pleasure," this refers to the subsiding of suffering.
It is due to the three causal conditions subsumed under the aforementioned cause of pleasure, and so forth.
Master Ji says:
"The three conditions are the faculty (indriya), the object (viṣaya), and karma that results in pleasant fruit; these constitute the three.
Furthermore, there is another distinct interpretation which adopts the specific meaning as explained previously."
In the *Śāstra*, among the distinctions between those pleasures that are intrinsic and those that are not intrinsic,
Jing states:
"Those bound to the three realms..."
The joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are collectively termed "bliss.
Regarding the joy and bliss found within the four factors and five factors of the first and second dhyānas respectively, they are both identical in being the feeling of joy (*saumanasya-vedanā*).
They are designated as "joy" from the perspective of bringing satisfaction to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
That which causes the ālayavijñāna to be gratified, or causes the five sense faculties (pañcendriya) that serve as its basis to be gratified, is called pleasure (*sukha*).
Now it is clarified that the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*) is also called pleasure.

In the third dhyāna there is the pleasure of mental consciousness;

from the fourth dhyāna upward, there is only equanimity and no pleasure. As for the statement that pleasure is bound to the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness: [it refers to the fact that] even though there is no [sensory] pleasure in the higher stages, the term "pleasure" is used because it exists as a mental factor associated with the mind in those realms.
That equanimity (*upekṣā*) which benefits both body and mind is collectively termed "pleasure" (*sukha*).
Regarding the pleasure that is the antidote to suffering: even when such sufferings as cold, heat, hunger, and thirst are extinguished, a perception of pleasure arises.
Jingyun asked:
"If it is like one who is cold obtaining fire, or one who is hungry obtaining food, then hot water and gruel are called 'remedies for suffering.'"
Should one take the fire, food, drink, and so forth to be the pleasure that counteracts suffering,
or should one take the pleasant sensation produced by that fire and so forth to be the pleasure that counteracts suffering?
If one takes fire and so forth [as the cause], it is not different from the aforementioned "causal pleasure" (*hetu-sukha*).
That is to say, the sense faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and so forth, which are capable of producing a pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), are called causal pleasure.
If one takes the pleasant feeling produced by fire and so forth as its essence, [it is likewise not different].
Thus, it is no different from experiencing pleasure. In the concluding section [of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*], it says:

"The pleasure that is the antidote to suffering is called 'pleasure' because it ceases suffering; it is not pleasure because it is not the cause of pleasure, nor is it the intrinsic nature of pleasure."
The answer is:

It is precisely the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā*) that arises simultaneously with the pleasant feeling produced by fire and so forth, which perceives the cessation of various sufferings; this is called the "antidote to suffering.

Furthermore, it may be understood as follows: when one is oppressed by the suffering of extreme hunger and thirst, obtaining coarse food and drink removes the suffering of hunger and thirst, yet pleasure is not produced; rather, only the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) arises.

The wisdom associated with equanimous feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*) that awakens to the absence of sufferings such as hunger and thirst is called the bliss of the antidote to suffering (*duḥkha-pratipakṣa-sukha*).

Regarding the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*), it is called the bliss of the severance of feeling (*vedanā-ccheda-sukha*). Jing says:

Based on the principle that, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the mental consciousness associated with equanimity is suffering due to conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), this ultimate suffering is temporarily pacified when one dwells in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); therefore, it is designated as "pleasure."
In truth, there is no conscious perception or feeling of the cessation of pleasure.
It is asked:
Does one who has extinguished the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception enter the untainted state of the meditative attainment of cessation?
The cessation-attainment (nirodha-samāpatti) is untainted (anāsrava). This, then, merely ceases the substance of untainted feeling;
although the substance of untainted feeling undergoes arising and ceasing, it is not the suffering of conditioned formations (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā).
How can it be said that when one dwells in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the ultimate suffering (*paramārthaduḥkha*) is extinguished?
The explanation is as follows:
when dwelling in the meditative absorption of cessation, one is proximate to the extinction of the untainted mind (*anāsravacitta*) and its mental factors (*caitasika*).
It is the distant cessation of the non-percipient (*asaṃjñin*) outflows (*āsrava*) and equanimity-feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
Now, based on this distant cessation, it is called the "cessation of outflows.

Because the perception and equanimity-feeling are subtle, they must be observed within meditative contemplation; only when observing the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) does one realize that the equanimity-feeling of the non-percipient state is itself the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), which is termed ultimate suffering (*paramārtha-duḥkha*).
Furthermore, it says:
"Just as with that unconditioned [state],
its reality is that one has already attained the unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling through the path of immediate succession."
After a long time, one finally attains that concentration.

At the moment of attaining that concentration, it is retrospectively designated by the name "unconditioned [state] of perception and feeling" (saṃjñāvedayita-nirodha) because it was obtained during the preceding path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga).
This present case is likewise so.
This concentration is exclusively an untainted preparatory stage (*anāsrava-prayoga*) and not tainted;
it is named "disgust for suffering" (*vidūṣaṇa-duḥkha*) because it takes that which is distantly loathed as its designation.
Although the distant mind is also tainted and wholesome, [it is so called for this reason].
From the perspective of ultimate truth, it is also suffering.
As for all other forms of happiness free from affliction and harm,
these refer to the happiness of renunciation, the happiness of seclusion, and the happiness of tranquility.
Because it is in accordance with the bliss of enlightenment;
because it is a portion of the bliss of enlightenment;
and because it is able to induce the bliss of enlightenment.
This is called the bliss of being free from affliction and harm.
From here below is the second section, which generally explains giving and not giving with respect to two types.
Within this, there are two parts.
First, it clarifies that mindfulness brings benefit and happiness to sentient beings and does not withhold from them what is unbeneficial and unpleasant.
Second, it clarifies that Bodhisattvas themselves also study and practice according to their own capacity.
Within the preceding section, there are again two parts:
first the general, then the specific.
Within the specific section, there are again two parts.
First, it clarifies that suffering and pleasure are bestowed according to what is beneficial, rather than according to one's desires;
second, it clarifies bestowing or not bestowing with respect to the five pleasures.
Within the first section, there are three further parts.
First, it clarifies that the bodhisattva, through wisdom, understands how to exhort those sentient beings to abandon unbeneficial pleasures.
Second, it clarifies that there are shared benefits which, even if the beings lack the desire for them, the bodhisattva should nevertheless relinquish his own [pleasures] to provide them.
If there are those who possess the three knowledges (*vidyā*) yet find pleasure in what is unbeneficial, they should be stripped of it.
Why? To explain further the meaning of bestowing and taking away, it is said:
"Therefore, when a bodhisattva finds that sentient beings delight in benefit, one should know that the intended meaning is that they delight in peace and happiness."
"Joy" refers to the desire for joy.
To bring benefit to others through that desire for joy is,
in effect, to bring happiness to others through that same desire for joy.
This is the preliminary mental state for bestowing benefit and happiness upon others.

Regarding the statement, "If one bestows benefit upon sentient beings, it should be known that this also bestows happiness," the subsequent passage clarifies the actual matter of bestowing both benefit and happiness.
Regarding the five types of pleasure, one should understand the distinction between what is to be given and what is not to be given:

all causes of happiness included within karma that yields desirable fruits in both the present life and future lives, up to and including that which is appropriate, should be bestowed upon sentient beings.
Jingyun: One portion of the three joys is bestowed exclusively [upon them],
because they are without fault.
Regarding the experience of pleasure therein, whether the causal pleasure comprised of the faculties, objects, and contact is granted or not,
it may be understood from the text as it stands. Jì (基) says:
Regarding these, one should investigate whether the first five types of happiness can or cannot be bestowed upon sentient beings.
If, within the first cause of happiness, one takes "karma conducive to happiness" as the referent,
then the happiness of the third, fourth, and fifth [causes] should be bestowed upon sentient beings unilaterally and need not be investigated further.

Regarding the cause—the two categories of objects for those of middling faculties within pleasure, as well as the second type of pleasant feeling—one should contemplate whether it is appropriate or inappropriate to give before bestowing it upon sentient beings;
herein lies an objection.
Just as there is a pleasure consisting in the cessation of the third type of suffering,
there is a sentient being who, previously afflicted by the suffering of poverty, was unable to commit transgressions; the Bodhisattva,
in order to eliminate that suffering, bestows wealth and treasures upon him.
When one currently acquires wealth and treasures, or even commits various transgressions through negligence,
does not the production of those various sins and defilements occur at the very time this pleasure is bestowed?

Furthermore, within pleasures that are free from affliction and harm— namely the pleasure of renunciation (*naiṣkramya-sukha*) and the pleasure of tranquility (*śānti-sukha*)— the meditative absorptions of the form realm (*rūpa-dhyāna*) are likewise both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena.
If one bestows [the teachings] upon sentient beings, they receive them and do not let them fall into neglect;
yet, though born in the realm of form, they give rise to craving for the flavor of meditative concentration and, failing to study the internal Dharma, reckon that state to be nirvana,
only to return again to the evil destinies.
If sentient beings who obtain it are neither without fault nor without defilement, for what reason do they not experience it with equanimity?
Why is it said that one may or may not bestow it upon those sentient beings, yet [the Buddha] grants it to all sentient beings unconditionally?
Furthermore, within the intrinsic nature of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), there are both outflows (*sāsrava*) and no-outflows (*anāsrava*).
Why is it not stated that the outflowing [feeling] involves discernment and reflection (*pratisaṃkhyāna-manasikāra*), while the non-outflowing [feeling] is exclusively bestowed?

Just as that karma which is pleasant in its cause and conduces to a pleasant fruit invariably bestows the causes of pleasure—namely, the sense faculties and their objects—it does not, however, invariably bestow them.
There are two types of such karma that is pleasant in its cause: that which bestows [the fruits] and that which does not.
Since there are two kinds of experience of pleasure, there should likewise be cases where it is given and where it is not.
Master Yuan said:
"Because karma conducive to pleasure includes that which is certain to be experienced, it is described as being 'certainly beneficial.'"
If there are sentient beings who give rise to karma conducive to suffering, the Bodhisattva does not bestow [the fruit];
if they give rise to karma conducive to happiness, he must certainly grant it.
Therefore, within that experience of happiness, the untainted feeling (*anāsrava-vedanā*)—which encompasses those who are certain to be benefited—is inexhaustible.
One must not teach in a partial manner,
for those to be transformed are immeasurable;
it is like the four dhyānas, which must certainly be bestowed upon those who are worthy.
The untainted (anāsrava) feeling is not like this. Question:
If there are those whose faculties are matured and who, desiring to enter the vision of the truths (satyadarśana), are capable of receiving the untainted [state], are they also determined?
"Why was it not given? The previous explanation is incorrect.
The meaning is as follows:
If one considers the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*),
even within the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of feeling (*vedanā*), one may distinguish it as being like pleasure; however,

because there is a distinction between the nature of being contaminated and the nature of being uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), uncontaminated feeling should not be categorized exclusively [with the former].
Furthermore, because there is a distinction between those who have entered the stages (*bhūmi*) and those who have not, one should not grant [the teaching] with absolute certainty.
Even if it were granted with certainty to those who have entered the stages,
since this would be contrasted with those who do not enter them, it is said that the former cannot serve as a precedent for the latter.
If that is so, how do you account for the pleasure of abandonment (*prahāṇasukha*) and the pleasure free from affliction (*avyābādhyasukha*)?

The answer is: because one contemplates them as being of a nature not to be felt (*avedanīya*), whether they be with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*). Thus, they are not the same as the three types of causal pleasure (*hetusukha*), which can be analyzed accordingly.
Furthermore, although the text speaks of the "bestowal" of the experience of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) and so forth exclusively [in that context],
it is understood by implication that the untainted experience (*anāsrava-vedanā*) is also bestowed;
for this is revealed through the elliptical nature of the phrasing, and thus the experience of pleasure is not explicitly mentioned.
